title: Aeneid - Book I, Proem
author: Publius Vergilius Maro
description: The opening of Virgil's epic, announcing its theme and invoking the Muse.

sections.latin:
Arma virumque cano, Troiae qui primus ab oris
Italiam, fato profugus, Laviniaque venit
litora, multum ille et terris iactatus et alto
vi superum saevae memorem Iunonis ob iram;
multa quoque et bello passus, dum conderet urbem,
inferretque deos Latio, genus unde Latinum,
Albanique patres, atque altae moenia Romae.
sections.translation: Arms and the man I sing, who first from the shores of Troy, exiled by fate, came to Italy and the Lavinian coast; much was he tossed about both on land and on the deep by the power of the gods above, on account of the unforgetting wrath of cruel Juno; much also did he suffer in war, until he could found a city and bring his gods to Latium, whence came the Latin race, the Alban fathers, and the walls of lofty Rome.

lineByLine.latin: Arma virumque cano, Troiae qui primus ab oris
lineByLine.translation: Arms and the man I sing, who first from the shores of Troy
lineByLine.notes: Arma virumque: hendiadys and echo of Homer's Iliad (arma/war) and Odyssey (virum/man)

lineByLine.translation: came to Italy, a fugitive by fate, and to the Lavinian
lineByLine.notes: fato profugus: ablative of cause; Lavinia refers to Lavinium, city founded by Aeneas

lineByLine.latin: litora, multum ille et terris iactatus et alto
lineByLine.translation: shores; much was that man tossed on both land and the deep

lineByLine.latin: vi superum saevae memorem Iunonis ob iram;
lineByLine.translation: by the power of the gods above, because of the unforgetting wrath of cruel Juno;
lineByLine.notes: superum: genitive plural (= superorum); memorem: Juno remembers the judgment of Paris

lineByLine.latin: multa quoque et bello passus, dum conderet urbem,
lineByLine.translation: having suffered much also in war, until he could found a city
lineByLine.notes: passus: perfect participle from patior; conderet: imperfect subjunctive in temporal clause

lineByLine.latin: inferretque deos Latio, genus unde Latinum,
lineByLine.translation: and bring his gods to Latium, whence the Latin race,
lineByLine.notes: deos: the Penates, household gods; unde: from which source

lineByLine.latin: Albanique patres, atque altae moenia Romae.
lineByLine.translation: and the Alban fathers, and the walls of lofty Rome.
lineByLine.notes: Albani patres: the kings of Alba Longa, ancestors of Romulus

sections.latin:
Musa, mihi causas memora, quo numine laeso,
quidve dolens, regina deum tot volvere casus
insignem pietate virum, tot adire labores
impulerit. Tantaene animis caelestibus irae?
sections.translation: Muse, recall to me the causes, by what offense to her divinity, or grieving for what, the queen of the gods drove a man distinguished for piety to undergo so many misfortunes, to face so many trials. Is there such great anger in heavenly minds?

lineByLine.latin: Musa, mihi causas memora, quo numine laeso,
lineByLine.translation: Muse, recall to me the causes, by what offense to her divinity,
lineByLine.notes: Invocation to the Muse; quo numine laeso: ablative absolute

lineByLine.latin: quidve dolens, regina deum tot volvere casus
lineByLine.translation: or grieving for what, the queen of gods [drove him] to undergo so many misfortunes
lineByLine.notes: regina deum: Juno; deum = deorum; volvere: infinitive with impulerit

lineByLine.latin: insignem pietate virum, tot adire labores
lineByLine.translation: a man distinguished for piety, to face so many trials
lineByLine.notes: pietate: ablative of specification; pietas = duty to gods, country, family

lineByLine.translation: drove [him]. Is there such great anger in heavenly minds?
lineByLine.notes: Rhetorical question: how can gods harbor such wrath?

historicalContext: Virgil composed the Aeneid over ten years (29-19 BCE) under Augustus's patronage. The epic links Rome's origins to Troy and legitimizes the Augustan regime by tracing Augustus's Julian family to Aeneas and Venus.
literaryFeatures: Opening echoes both Homeric epics: Iliad (arms/war) and Odyssey (man/wandering)
Dactylic hexameter with masterful use of spondees for gravity
Central theme of pietas (duty to gods, family, country)
Juno's wrath parallels Poseidon's anger in the Odyssey
